title: The Gulf Stream, step by step
alt: NASA's picture of the south-east United States and the western North Atlantic, spring 2023. Fine white flow lines cover the blue sea. A thick bright band runs north between Florida and the Bahamas, follows the coast, then turns east into loops and swirls.

wave.label: A wave
wave.text: A wave: the tone bobs up and down but stays in the middle. The water rises and falls in one place.

current.label: A current
current.text: A current: the tone travels steadily from your left ear to your right. The water is carried along.

east.label: East
east.text: East: the tone moves from your left ear to your right.

west.label: West
west.text: West: the tone moves from your right ear to your left.

slow.label: Slow
slow.text: Slow: a few ticks a second.

fast.label: Fast
fast.text: Fast: quick ticks, like the middle of the Gulf Stream.

together.label: North, fast
together.text: Both together: the tone rises for north, while quick ticks play for fast water.

steps.title: What is an ocean current?
steps.text: An ocean current is water that keeps flowing the same way, like a river in the sea. A wave is different. When a wave passes, the water mostly rises and falls in about the same place: a floating ball bobs up and down and stays put. In a current, the ball would be carried away. Currents can carry warm water thousands of kilometres. Two sounds show the difference.

steps.title: Our example: the Gulf Stream
steps.text: Our example is the Gulf Stream, one of the fastest currents on Earth. It flows between Florida and the Bahamas, runs north along the east coast of the United States, then turns out across the Atlantic, carrying warm water from the tropics. Everything you hear in this lesson is measured from NASA's film Perpetual Ocean 2, from 17 March 2023 to 19 June 2023, while NASA's camera holds still over the Gulf Stream. We measured which way NASA's white flow lines move, and how fast.

steps.title: The direction sound
steps.text: First, direction: which way the water goes. Imagine you are floating in the sea, facing north. The direction sound is a short tone that travels the way the water goes. Water flowing north: the tone rises. Flowing south: it falls. Flowing east: it moves from your left ear to your right. Flowing west: from your right ear to your left. Headphones help with left and right.

steps.title: Direction, place 1 of 4: off Miami
steps.text: Off Miami, the Gulf Stream squeezes between Florida and the Bahamas. Here the water flows north.

steps.title: Direction, place 2 of 4: off Georgia
steps.text: Further north, off Georgia, the coast bends away to the east, and the current bends with it. Here the water flows northeast.

steps.title: Direction, place 3 of 4: off the Carolinas
steps.text: Off the Carolinas, the current leaves the coast and heads out to sea. Here the water flows east.

steps.title: Direction, place 4 of 4: far out in the Atlantic
steps.place: far out in the Atlantic, south of the stream
steps.text: Now far out in the Atlantic, south of the stream and east of the Bahamas. Here the water drifts west, almost the opposite way. The Gulf Stream is one side of a giant loop of currents that turns slowly around the North Atlantic.

steps.title: The speed sound
steps.text: Next, speed: how fast the water moves. The speed sound is a run of soft ticks, like drops passing you. The faster the water, the faster the ticks. The ticks stay in the middle and keep one pitch, so you hear speed alone. Speeds are compared with the fastest water in this part of NASA's film.

steps.title: Speed across the current
steps.place: a line from the coast at Cape Canaveral, Florida, out to sea
steps.text: Now cross the current off Cape Canaveral, Florida, from the coast straight out to sea. You will hear 7 places, each named by how far it is from the coast. Listen for the ticks to speed up in the middle of the stream, then slow down again.
steps.after: The fastest water was about 115 kilometres from the coast. The Gulf Stream is a narrow, fast river inside slower water.

steps.title: Changes over time
steps.text: Last, change. Currents shift from week to week. Now we stay in one place and listen to it every 8 days, 12 times, from 17 March 2023 to 19 June 2023. Each time you hear both sounds you have learned at once: the tone for direction, and ticks for speed. The date is said first.

steps.title: Change, place 1 of 2: a steady place
steps.place: the middle of the Gulf Stream, off Cape Canaveral
steps.text: First, the middle of the Gulf Stream off Cape Canaveral. Listen: does the direction change?
steps.after: All 12 times, the water flowed north, though its speed changed, from 48 to 100 percent of the fastest. Near Florida, the Gulf Stream holds its course.

steps.title: Change, place 2 of 2: a restless place
steps.place: out at sea, east of the Carolinas
steps.text: Now a place out at sea, east of the Carolinas, where the current snakes and swirls. The same 12 times, 8 days apart.
steps.after: Here the direction kept turning: west, southwest, south, southeast, east and northeast. A bend in the current, called a meander, drifted past, and swirls called eddies broke off it. Currents are steady in some places and restless in others.

steps.title: What you learned, and the full tour
steps.text: You learned that a current is water that keeps moving one way, unlike a wave. The Gulf Stream flows north along Florida, then turns east across the Atlantic, while slow water far to the south drifts back west. It is fastest in a narrow middle, steady near Florida and restless further out. The full tour, in the player, is NASA's world map of every ocean's surface currents, March 2007 to March 2008. A scan line moves from west to east across it, and only what is under the line plays. Its sounds differ from this lesson's: a harp note rings where the line crosses a strong current, and a low hum follows all the moving water under the line. There, high and in your left ear means north, low and in your right ear means south. The Gulf Stream comes about a third of the way across.

caveat: Directions and speeds are measured from how NASA's white flow lines move in the film, while NASA's camera holds still. Speeds are compared with the fastest water in this view; they are not metres per second. NASA's film shows a computer model of the ocean (ECCO2), not single measurements.
